newsitem.title: ISRAEL: New issues market springs back to life in Tel Aviv.
newsitem.headline: New issues market springs back to life in Tel Aviv.

text.p: Israeli companies are finally ending their three-year old fixation on Wall Street and coming home again to raise money on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, brokers and underwriters said on Thursday.

A slew of real estate companies, like Azorim Investment Development and Construction and Industrial Buildings Ltd, are making offerings, while the government is raising 1.2 billion shekels ($350 million) from shares and warrants in Bank Leumi and Israel Discount Bank.

Even a high-tech company, Comfy Interactive Toys, has opted to float in Tel Aviv this month rather than in New York, where almost all the initial public offerings of Israeli technology companies have been made.

"It's a good time to raise capital," said Adam Ofek, chief executive officer of Solid Capital Markets. "There's a lot of money in the market which has entered in the last six months and is looking for a place to go."

Joseph Riback, deputy managing director of Poalim Capital Markets, estimates 15 to 20 other companies are now planning Tel Aviv offers and as many as 40 are thinking about it. The government hopes to float shares in Bezeq Israel Telecom this summer.

The revival of the new issues markets comes on the heels of a rally in stock prices that began at the end of last year. Although the run-up has tapered off since February and trading volumes have fallen, Ofek said the Tel Aviv market has retained its underlying strength.
The simultaneous high trading volumes in equities and inflation-indexed bonds pointed to a continued flow of new money, he said.

"The revival of the new issues market is another sign that the bear is really behind us," added Eli Nahum of Zannex Securities. "We are really in a bull market where people can raise money in the primary market."

Analysts said property companies were leading the wave of new offerings because they were most in need of cash. The central bank has clamped down on construction lending out of concern that banks are overexposed to the sector, forcing developers to turn to the market.
"They're more eager than other companies to raise money," said Nahum.
But he and other analysts said they expected other sectors to begin raising money, too.

The preference for convertible bonds and warrants, Nahum said, reflected lingering concerns about whether the bull market is sustainable and companies' reluctance to sell equity at comparatively low valuations.

Typical of the recent spate of offerings is Osif Investment and Development Ltd, which made an offering of convertibles and warrants valued at 136.5 million shekels, fully diluted. The offering includes no stock.
"You wouldn't want to dilute yourself at this market level, when the company is worth one third or one half its underlying value," Nahum said.

Ofek said the trend toward lower interest rates also caused issuers to favour bonds. The Bank of Israel has lowered the base rate 3.1 percentage points since last summer and will continue to ease them as inflation falls, he said.
But analysts said they expect the market's taste for equity to grow towards the end of the year.
"We're starting to see more equities, but it may take time," said Riback. "There's still a lot of concern about stocks after the long slump."

Even with its recent revival, Tel Aviv poses no threat to New York for Israeli public offerings. Comfy aside, high-tech companies still prefer the international exposure and higher valuations they get in New York.
Ofek said low-tech companies would also continue to pursue overseas listings because U.S. money managers prefer to hold U.S.-listed companies.
"There will be a growing market capitalisation in Israel and the U.S.," he said. "I don't see one precluding the other."
($1 = 3.40 shekels)
